subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A 21-year-old college soccer player twists his right knee while planting his foot. Arthroscopy demonstrates a ligament running from the lateral femoral condyle to the anterior tibia. Which structure is being described?
question: Which structure runs from the lateral femoral condyle to the anterior tibia?
explanation_correct: The LAMP mnemonic gives the cruciate attachments: Lateral femoral condyle to Anterior tibia is the ACL, and Medial femoral condyle to Posterior tibia is the PCL. The ACL resists anterior translation of the tibia on the femur. A planting and twisting mechanism is classic for an ACL tear.

explanation_incorrect.A: The PCL runs from the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibia, the opposite diagonal from the structure described.
explanation_incorrect.C: The MCL is a medial-sided capsular ligament spanning the medial femoral condyle to the medial tibia, not a cruciate crossing to the anterior tibia.
explanation_incorrect.D: The LCL runs from the lateral femoral condyle to the fibular head and resists varus stress; it does not attach to the anterior tibia.
explanation_incorrect.E: The lateral meniscus is a C-shaped fibrocartilage on the tibial plateau, not a ligament coursing from femoral condyle to tibia.

educationalObjective: Recall the LAMP mnemonic for cruciate ligament femoral and tibial attachments.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A 24-year-old man hears a pop after a cutting injury and develops an immediate hemarthrosis. With the knee flexed to 90 degrees, the examiner notes that the tibia glides anteriorly relative to the femur compared with the uninjured side.
question: Which ligament is most likely torn?

options.text: Posterior horn of the medial meniscus

explanation_correct: The anterior drawer sign is positive when the tibia glides anteriorly with the knee at 90 degrees and indicates an ACL tear. The ACL normally prevents anterior translation of the tibia. A pop with immediate swelling after a cutting mechanism is classic, and the Lachman test is the equivalent maneuver performed at 30 degrees.

explanation_incorrect.A: PCL injury produces a posterior drawer sign with posterior gliding of the tibia, not anterior translation.
explanation_incorrect.B: MCL injury is detected with valgus stress and medial joint space widening, not anterior drawer translation.
explanation_incorrect.C: LCL injury is detected with varus stress and lateral joint space widening.
explanation_incorrect.E: Meniscal tears are evaluated with McMurray testing and joint-line tenderness, not the anterior drawer maneuver.

educationalObjective: Associate anterior drawer at 90 degrees with ACL insufficiency.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A 19-year-old athlete sustains a noncontact knee injury. The examiner flexes the knee to 30 degrees and applies an anterior force to the proximal tibia, appreciating increased translation relative to the other side.
question: Which test is being performed, and what does a positive result indicate?
explanation_correct: The Lachman test is performed at 30 degrees of knee flexion and assesses anterior tibial translation, indicating ACL insufficiency. It is more sensitive than the anterior drawer test, which is performed at 90 degrees. Both Lachman and anterior drawer evaluate the ACL but are distinguished by the flexion angle.

explanation_incorrect.B: The Lachman test evaluates the ACL, not the PCL; PCL injury is assessed with the posterior drawer.
explanation_incorrect.C: The anterior drawer test is performed at 90 degrees of flexion, not 30 degrees.
explanation_incorrect.D: The posterior drawer test checks the PCL and assesses posterior, not anterior, tibial translation.
explanation_incorrect.E: McMurray testing stresses the menisci with rotation and varus/valgus force, not anterior translation at 30 degrees.

educationalObjective: Identify the Lachman test at 30 degrees as an ACL integrity check.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A high school football player is tackled from the lateral side so that the knee is forced into valgus. On examination at 30 degrees of flexion, there is medial joint space widening and pain without a firm endpoint.
question: Which ligament is most likely injured?
explanation_correct: Valgus stress at 30 degrees that widens the medial joint space indicates MCL injury. A valgus (lateral) force opens the medial side of the knee. The MCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress, especially at 30 degrees of flexion.

explanation_incorrect.A: The ACL resists anterior tibial translation and is tested with Lachman or anterior drawer maneuvers, not valgus stress.
explanation_incorrect.B: The PCL resists posterior tibial translation and is tested with the posterior drawer.
explanation_incorrect.D: The LCL is the restraint to varus stress; a lateral blow producing valgus force injures the MCL.
explanation_incorrect.E: The lateral meniscus is stressed by internal rotation with varus force on McMurray testing.

educationalObjective: Link valgus stress with medial joint widening to MCL injury.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A 28-year-old woman sustains a direct blow to the medial aspect of the knee, producing a varus force. Examination at 30 degrees of flexion demonstrates lateral joint space widening and tenderness along the lateral knee.
question: Which ligament is most likely torn?
explanation_correct: Varus stress at 30 degrees widens the lateral joint space and indicates LCL injury. A medial (varus) force opens the lateral side of the knee. The LCL is the primary lateral restraint and is tested with varus stress, in contrast to the MCL with valgus stress.

explanation_incorrect.A: The MCL is injured by valgus stress with medial widening, the opposite mechanism.
explanation_incorrect.B: The ACL is tested with anterior translation maneuvers, not varus stress.
explanation_incorrect.C: The PCL is tested with the posterior drawer maneuver.
explanation_incorrect.D: The medial meniscus is stressed by external rotation with valgus force on McMurray testing.

educationalObjective: Link varus stress with lateral joint widening to LCL injury.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Knee examination: ligaments and meniscal tests
vignette: A 35-year-old man has joint-line pain and intermittent catching after a twisting knee injury. During flexion and extension, the examiner internally rotates the tibia and applies a varus force, reproducing pain and a palpable pop.
question: Which structure is most likely torn?
explanation_correct: The McMurray test uses the LIME mnemonic: internal rotation with varus force stresses the lateral meniscus, whereas external rotation with valgus force stresses the medial meniscus. Reproducing pain or popping with internal rotation and varus indicates a lateral meniscal tear. The menisci are fibrocartilaginous shock absorbers on the tibial plateau.

explanation_incorrect.A: A medial meniscal tear is stressed by external rotation and valgus force, the opposite of this maneuver.
explanation_incorrect.C: ACL injury is detected by Lachman or anterior drawer testing, not rotational McMurray maneuvers.
explanation_incorrect.D: PCL injury is detected by the posterior drawer test.
explanation_incorrect.E: MCL injury is detected by valgus stress with medial joint widening.

educationalObjective: Apply the LIME mnemonic to localize a meniscal tear on McMurray testing.
